steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our video instance segmentation paper, VISAGE. Motivate it with the over-reliance of online query-based VIS methods on positional cues, introduce our appearance-guided approach and simplified tracker, and summarize what it achieves.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- VIS task; online vs offline; online methods dominant
- Query-based online VIS and its tracking failures
- Observation: queries rely on position, not appearance
- VISAGE: appearance queries + contrastive loss
- Simplified tracker with memory bank
- Properties and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- VIS
  - classification, segmentation, tracking of instances through video
  - online (per-frame) vs offline (per-clip)
  - better frame-level detectors -> online increasingly dominant
- Query-based online VIS
  - detectors drive video accuracy; built on query-based detectors
  - queries represent object-wise info
  - online VIS reuses queries; big gains on benchmarks; propagation or matching strategies
  - still imperfect under shot changes, trajectory intersections (Fig. 1)
- Observation
  - object-wise info imbalanced: heavy positional, weak appearance
  - previous methods keep spatial order of previous predictions (Fig. 1)
  - analysis: horizontally flipped images -> two-frame pseudo videos
  - association errors despite distinct exteriors (top of Fig. 2)
  - need to consider appearance
- VISAGE
  - appearance cues to distinguish instances
  - branch with mask pooling: appearance queries from predicted masks of object queries
  - each appearance query captures visual features of its object
  - contrastive loss to distinguish instances across frames
- Tracker
  - minimize heuristic procedures
  - previous methods: multiple refinement steps, handcrafted thresholds, selected queries only
  - many dataset-tuned hyperparameters
  - ours: far fewer hyperparameters (tracklet init/delete thresholds, NMS, ...)
  - query-matching online methods only see adjacent frames -> simple memory bank for temporal awareness
- Properties/results
  - new paradigm: appearance info for association
  - better in complex tracking than spatially-dependent methods (Fig. 1 (a)); bottom of Fig. 2
  - large-scale pseudo dataset: beats established methods by a large margin
  - simplified tracker with history of object + appearance queries: competitive on all benchmarks
  - state-of-the-art on YouTubeVIS-19/21 and OVIS

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) is a challenging task that needs classification, segmentation, and tracking of distinct instances through a video sequence. Current VIS studies can mostly be divided into two approaches, online and offline, depending on whether the video is processed per-frame or per-clip. Recently, as frame-level object detectors have advanced, online methods have become more and more dominant in the VIS field.

Detectors directly affect accuracy in the video domain, so recent online models are mostly built on powerful query-based detectors. These detectors decode image information spatially and are designed to represent object-wise information with queries. So online VIS methods reuse these queries from the detectors, and they have achieved big improvements on several challenging benchmarks, mostly using either propagation or matching strategies. But tracking in complex scenarios like shot changes or trajectory intersections (Fig. 1) is still not perfect, and this lowers the overall accuracy.

Looking at these failure cases, we see that the object-wise information in the queries is very imbalanced: it relies heavily on positional cues and reflects appearance less. As Fig. 1 shows, previous query-based VIS methods tend to keep the spatial order of their previous predictions in the current predictions. To support this, we do additional analyses where we horizontally flip images to make two-frame pseudo videos. The existing models make association errors even though the objects have distinct exterior patterns, as shown at the top of Fig. 2, which shows they depend on object locations. Since there are many scenarios that cannot be fully handled with this imbalanced information, models need to take object appearances into account.

- VISAGE
  - appearance cues to distinguish instances
  - mask pooling branch -> appearance queries from predicted masks
  - contrastive loss across frames
- Tracker
  - previous methods: refinement steps, handcrafted thresholds, many hyperparameters
  - ours: far fewer hyperparameters (tracklet thresholds, NMS)
  - memory bank for temporal awareness beyond adjacent frames
- Properties/results
  - appearance for association; better in complex tracking (Fig. 1 (a), bottom of Fig. 2)
  - large-scale pseudo dataset, big margin over established methods
  - competitive on all benchmarks; state-of-the-art on YouTubeVIS-19/21 and OVIS

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) is a challenging task that needs classification, segmentation, and tracking of distinct instances through a video sequence. Current VIS studies can mostly be divided into two approaches, online and offline, depending on whether the video is processed per-frame or per-clip. Recently, as frame-level object detectors have advanced, online methods have become more and more dominant in the VIS field.

Detectors directly affect accuracy in the video domain, so recent online models are mostly built on powerful query-based detectors. These detectors decode image information spatially and are designed to represent object-wise information with queries. So online VIS methods reuse these queries from the detectors, and they have achieved big improvements on several challenging benchmarks, mostly using either propagation or matching strategies. But tracking in complex scenarios like shot changes or trajectory intersections (Fig. 1) is still not perfect, and this lowers the overall accuracy.

Looking at these failure cases, we see that the object-wise information in the queries is very imbalanced: it relies heavily on positional cues and reflects appearance less. As Fig. 1 shows, previous query-based VIS methods tend to keep the spatial order of their previous predictions in the current predictions. To support this, we do additional analyses where we horizontally flip images to make two-frame pseudo videos. The existing models make association errors even though the objects have distinct exterior patterns, as shown at the top of Fig. 2, which shows they depend on object locations. Since there are many scenarios that cannot be fully handled with this imbalanced information, models need to take object appearances into account.

We introduce VISAGE (Video Instance Segmentation with Appearance-Guided Enhancement), a method that uses appearance cues as an important indicator for telling instances apart. In our approach we add a streamlined branch that uses mask pooling to generate appearance queries from the predicted mask of object queries. This way each appearance query captures the visual features of its object, which gives a more complete representation and better tracking accuracy. To make queries more discriminative, we also add a contrastive loss, which improves the model's ability to distinguish instances across different frames.

We also introduce a streamlined tracker that is designed to rely on heuristic procedures as little as possible. Previous methods use multiple refinement steps to remove redundant mask proposals and use handcrafted threshold values to build tracklets accurately. With this processing, only selected queries go into the matching process. These complex tracker configurations improve tracking accuracy, but they also depend on many hyperparameters, and each of these can be tuned heuristically for specific datasets. To reduce this dependence, our method simplifies the tracker and greatly reduces the number of hyperparameters needed, like threshold values for initializing and deleting tracklets, non-maximum suppression (NMS), and others. However, query-matching online methods still lack temporal information, since they only know about adjacent frames. We handle this limitation with a simple memory bank that gives temporal awareness.

Even though our approach is simple, VISAGE has many desirable properties. Our method introduces a new paradigm in query-based VIS by emphasizing that appearance information plays a crucial role in object association. With appearance-based guidance it performs better in complex tracking scenarios than previous methods, which often misidentify objects because they depend too much on spatial information, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). It successfully uses appearance information, as shown at the bottom of Fig. 2, and it has been validated on our proposed large-scale pseudo dataset, where it outperforms established methods by a large margin. Also, with its simplified tracker that makes effective use of the past history of both object and appearance queries, our method shows competitive performance on all benchmark datasets. VISAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance on three standard benchmarks: YouTubeVIS-19/21 and OVIS.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) is a challenging task that requires classification, segmentation, and tracking of distinct instances throughout a video sequence [1]. Current VIS studies can be primarily categorized into online and offline approaches, depending on whether a video is processed per frame or per clip. Recently, advances in frame-level object detectors have made online methods increasingly dominant in the VIS field.

As detectors directly impact accuracy in the video domain, recent online models are primarily built on powerful query-based detectors [2,3]. These detectors spatially decode image information and are designed to represent object-wise information using queries. Online VIS methods therefore reuse these queries and have achieved substantial improvements on multiple challenging benchmarks [4,5], mostly by adopting either propagation [6,7] or matching [8,9,10] strategies. However, tracking in complex scenarios such as shot changes or trajectory intersections (Fig. 1) remains imperfect, degrading overall accuracy.

Examining these failure cases, we observe that the object-wise information of the queries is significantly imbalanced: it relies heavily on positional cues and reflects appearance less. As demonstrated in Fig. 1, previous query-based VIS methods [6,10,8,9,11] tend to maintain the spatial order of previous predictions in their current predictions. To support this argument, we conduct additional analyses in which we horizontally flip images to generate two-frame pseudo videos. The existing models make association errors despite the objects' distinct exterior patterns, as shown at the top of Fig. 2, highlighting their dependence on object locations. Since multiple scenarios cannot be fully handled with such imbalanced information, models need to take object appearances into consideration.

We introduce VISAGE (Video Instance Segmentation with Appearance-Guided Enhancement), a method that leverages appearance cues as a crucial indicator for distinguishing instances. Our approach introduces a streamlined branch that employs mask pooling to generate appearance queries from the predicted masks of object queries. This enables each appearance query to capture the visual features of its corresponding object, providing a more comprehensive representation for improved tracking accuracy. To refine query discrimination, we integrate a contrastive loss [12,13,14], which enhances the model’s ability to distinguish between instances across different frames.

Additionally, we introduce a streamlined tracker designed to minimize reliance on heuristic procedures as far as feasible. Previous methods [9,10] employ multiple refinement steps to remove redundant mask proposals and adopt handcrafted threshold values for accurate tracklet construction, so that only selectively chosen queries enter the matching process. Although these complex tracker configurations enhance tracking accuracy, they create a dependency on numerous hyperparameters, each of which can be tailored heuristically to specific datasets. To alleviate this dependence, our method streamlines the tracker and dramatically reduces the number of required hyperparameters, such as threshold values for initializing and deleting tracklets and non-maximum suppression (NMS). Nonetheless, query-matching online methods inherently lack temporal information, as they are only aware of adjacent frames; we address this limitation with a simple memory bank that facilitates temporal awareness.

Despite its simplicity, VISAGE has many desirable properties. Our method introduces a new paradigm in query-based VIS by emphasizing the crucial role of appearance information for object association. Guided by appearance, it performs better in complex tracking scenarios than previous methods, which often misidentify objects due to an excessive dependence on spatial information, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). It successfully leverages appearance information, as illustrated at the bottom of Fig. 2, and has been validated on our proposed large-scale pseudo dataset, where it outperforms established methods [6,10] by a large margin. Furthermore, with a simplified tracker that effectively uses the past history of both object and appearance queries, our method demonstrates competitive performance across all benchmark datasets. Notably, VISAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance on three standard benchmarks: YouTubeVIS-19/21 [1,15] and OVIS [4].
